newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - U.S. fed funds rise seen in Q1, then fall.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - U.S. fed funds rise seen in Q1, then fall.

text.p: A growing economy above the trend rate coupled with low unemployment will induce the Federal Reserve to tighten short-term interest rates by the end of the first-quarter 1997, according to economists in a Reuters quarterly U.S. economic survey.

Asked last week to forecast the federal funds rate eight quarters forward, pundits predicted it would gradually rise in the first and second quarters of 1997, hold steady throughout the third quarter of 1997, and head south thereafter.

Experts' consensus mean estimates are for a fed funds rate close to 5.50 percent by the end of the first-quarter 1997 and close to 5.0 percent by the end of third-quarter 1998. The current fed funds rate is set at 5.25 percent.

The survey, however, evoked fewer responses for the most distant time frames, with 23 respondents offering forecasts for the end of fourth-quarter 1996, 24 projecting through third-quarter 1997 and a scant nine adumbrating through the third-quarter 1998.
Despite the dwindling number of long-range forecasts, the numerous short-range projections tell a convincing tale -- the Fed is expected to move to prevent inflation and curb swift economic growth.

"Above-trend growth, a moderate pickup in inflation and a continually falling unemployment rate," will lead the Fed to tighten gradually over the next few quarters, said Sally Kleinman, senior domestic economist at Chase Securities Inc.
The Fed has delayed tightening policy so far, which means that interest rates have not risen to levels that would start to slow the economy, noted Kleinman.
She said that combination of events "will cause the Fed to tighten gradually, not an aggressive tightening, but a gradual tightening."

Waldo Best, senior economist at BZW Securities Inc, also called for an increase in short-term interest rates early next year. His prediction is based on the notion that "the economy is running much closer to its potential (growth rate ) than it has been over the past."
Any number above the potential rate is going to close the output gap, said Best. And the output gap -- the difference between potential and actual GDP -- is likely to narrow.

The Commerce Department last month said second-quarter seasonally adjusted final Gross Domestic Product (GDP) rose 4.7 percent. Best said he sees the potential sustainable GDP growth rate at 2.3 percent.

"Every time we have gotten this close to a potential GDP in the past, the Fed has tightened," Best said, adding "that is the reason the market was anticipating it at the September (monetary policy) meeting."
With the economy running close to what many consider full employment at the current unemployment rate of 5.2 percent, "we are in trouble -- in terms of inflation," added Best.

With bad inflation news and a revival in consumer spending looming, the Fed may need to tighten in the second quarter of 1997, according to Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp.

However, after a hawkish monetary policy prevails, Liro said, he sees the Fed easing by the end of the fourth quarter of 1997. "That is predicated on a couple of things," he said, adding that the Fed must tighten credit and the yield curve needs to flatten.
Once the yield curve flattens, interest-rate sensitive sectors will weaken, said Liro. "That should move the Fed from that modest amount of tightening we expect, to becoming accommodative," he added.
Easing is sort of a back door for the Fed, said BZW's Best. "You can always overtighten so to speak because you can always ease your way out of trouble (afterward)."
